## Welcome

Medical imaging plays an important role in diagnosing and monitoring health conditions. However, hospitals can report different results for the same imaging measures.

This project explores outpatient imaging data from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), focusing on two measures:

- **OP-10:** Abdomen CT Use of Contrast Material.
- **OP-39:** Breast Cancer Screening Recall Rates.

As someone interested in becoming an ultrasound technician, I wanted to explore how medical imaging practices vary across hospitals in the United States.

## Imaging at a Glance

These statistics are calculated directly from the CMS dataset.

```{r}
#| results: asis

library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)

imaging_url <- "https://data.cms.gov/provider-data/sites/default/files/resources/d0134a9a89e59d49426cf5a2ad063b60_1792599881/Outpatient_Imaging_Efficiency-Hospital.csv"

imaging <- read_csv(imaging_url, show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(Score = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(Score))) |>
  dplyr::filter(
    !is.na(Score),
    `Measure ID` %in% c("OP-10", "OP-39")
  )

summary_stats <- imaging |>
  group_by(`Measure ID`) |>
  summarise(
    hospitals = n_distinct(`Facility ID`),
    median_score = median(Score),
    q25 = quantile(Score, 0.25),
    q75 = quantile(Score, 0.75),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

total_hospitals <- n_distinct(imaging$`Facility ID`)

ct <- summary_stats |> dplyr::filter(`Measure ID` == "OP-10")
mammo <- summary_stats |> dplyr::filter(`Measure ID` == "OP-39")

cat('<div class="imaging-stats">')

cat(sprintf(
  '<div class="imaging-stat"><strong>%s</strong><span>Hospitals with available imaging scores</span></div>',
  format(total_hospitals, big.mark = ",")
))

cat(sprintf(
  '<div class="imaging-stat"><strong>%.1f%%</strong><span>Median OP-10 CT score</span></div>',
  ct$median_score
))

cat(sprintf(
  '<div class="imaging-stat"><strong>%.1f%%</strong><span>Median OP-39 recall rate</span></div>',
  mammo$median_score
))

cat('</div>')
```

## Distribution of Imaging Measures

The following visualization compares the distribution of reported percentages across hospitals.

```{r}
imaging_plot <- imaging |>
  mutate(
    Measure = case_when(
      `Measure ID` == "OP-10" ~ "OP-10: Abdomen CT",
      `Measure ID` == "OP-39" ~ "OP-39: Breast Screening"
    )
  )

medians <- imaging_plot |>
  group_by(Measure) |>
  summarise(median_score = median(Score), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(imaging_plot, aes(x = Score, fill = Measure)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1.5, color = "white", alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_vline(
    data = medians,
    aes(xintercept = median_score),
    linetype = "dashed",
    linewidth = 0.8,
    inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~Measure, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#167d8d", "#d87850")) +
  labs(
    title = "Hospital-Reported Outpatient Imaging Percentages",
    subtitle = "Distribution of OP-10 and OP-39 scores",
    x = "Reported percentage (%)",
    y = "Number of hospitals",
    caption = "Source: CMS Outpatient Imaging Efficiency – Hospital"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```

## What Can We Learn?

The distributions show that reported imaging percentages vary across hospitals. Most hospitals cluster within a relatively narrow range, while some report much higher percentages.

These differences are worth exploring, but they do not automatically indicate better or worse care. Clinical circumstances and patient populations can influence reported measures.

The two measures describe different processes and should not be combined into an overall hospital quality score.
